Humiliation of Christ
hyoo-mil-ee-AY-shun uv kryst
noun phrase (an estate of Christ)
From the Latin humiliatio, a making low, from humus, the ground; the estate in which the Son of God lowered Himself for our salvation, as the catechisms confess.

Biblical Definition

The humiliation of Christ is the first of His two estates as Mediator, the condition of lowliness into which the eternal Son descended for the salvation of His people, answered afterward by His estate of exaltation. The Shorter Catechism summarizes it: Christ's humiliation consisted in His being born, and that in a low condition, made under the law, undergoing the miseries of this life, the wrath of God, and the cursed death of the cross; in being buried, and continuing under the power of death for a time. The apostle traces its descent: though He was in the form of God, He made Himself of no reputation, took the form of a servant, was made in the likeness of men, and being found in fashion as a man, He humbled Himself and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross. Though He was rich, yet for our sakes He became poor, that we through His poverty might be rich. Isaiah foresaw the depth of it: despised and rejected of men, a man of sorrows and acquainted with grief. The dictionary holds the humiliation as real and voluntary: the Son did not lay aside His deity but veiled His glory and took our nature with all its sinless weaknesses, descending step by step from the manger to the grave. The estate is the measure of His love and the ground of His sympathy, for the Mediator who saves us first stooped beneath us, that He might lift us to where He now reigns.

Webster 1828 Definition

The first estate of Christ the Mediator—His descent into lowliness through incarnation, a low birth, the miseries of life, the wrath of God, the cursed death of the cross, burial, and continuing under death—answered by His exaltation.

HUMILIATION OF CHRIST, noun phrase. [Latin humiliatio, a making low.] The estate of lowliness into which the Son of God descended to save His people.

It included His being born in a low condition and made under the law.

It included the miseries of this life, the wrath of God, and the cursed death of the cross.

It included His burial and His continuing under the power of death for a time.

It was voluntary and real: He made Himself of no reputation and humbled Himself (Philippians 2:7-8).

Key Scripture

Php 2:7 — "But made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant, and was made in the likeness of men:"

Php 2:8 — "And being found in fashion as a man, he humbled himself, and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross."

2 Co 8:9 — "For ye know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that, though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, that ye through his poverty might be rich."

Isa 53:3 — "He is despised and rejected of men; a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief: and we hid as it were our faces from him; he was despised, and we esteemed him not."

Modern Corruption

The kenotic error supposes the Son emptied Himself of deity in His humiliation, and the prosperity gospel inverts the whole estate, despising the lowliness God exalts.

expand to see more

A persistent error reads “made himself of no reputation” (literally “emptied himself”) as though the Son laid aside His divine attributes or even His deity in becoming man. The dictionary, with the catholic creeds and the Reformed confessions, rejects this kenotic theology. The Son emptied Himself not by subtraction of His Godhead but by the addition of our nature and the veiling of His glory; He remained fully God while becoming truly man. To suppose otherwise is to deny the immutability of God and to leave us with a Saviour who is less than divine at the very point we need Him most.

The prosperity gospel commits the opposite corruption, despising the whole estate of humiliation. It preaches a Christ of wealth and ease and bids His people seek the same, when the Lord Himself, being rich, became poor for our sakes, and entered glory only through the door of suffering and the cross. The dictionary recovers the pattern the apostle sets: the mind that was in Christ Jesus, who humbled Himself before He was exalted, so that the servant is not above his Lord, and the road to glory still runs through lowliness, obedience, and the cross.

Hebrew Roots

From the Latin humilis (low, lowly), from humus (the ground); the Greek etapeinosen heauton (“he humbled himself,” Philippians 2:8) and ekenosen (“made of no reputation”) frame the estate.

expand to see more

Humilis, Latin, low or lowly, from humus, the earth or ground.

Tapeinoo, Greek, to make low or humble, of Christ humbling Himself unto death.

Kenoo, Greek, to empty, “made himself of no reputation” (by addition and veiling, not subtraction of deity).

Morphe doulou, Greek, “the form of a servant,” the nature He truly assumed.

The catechetical pairing of humiliation with exaltation orders the two estates of the Mediator.

Usage

"The teacher set the humiliation of Christ against the prosperity gospel, for the Lord became poor to make us rich."

"He guarded the catechism's words, that the Son emptied Himself by taking our nature, not by laying down His deity."

"She meditated on the descent from the form of God to the death of the cross, and worshipped the love that stooped so low."
